title: "Acceptance Criteria Written After the Fact" (Failure Pattern)
snippet: Writing criteria only after implementation is complete, inverting the artifact's purpose of forcing clarity before work begins.

title: "Design Thinking as Linear Checklist" (Failure Pattern)
snippet: Treating the five stages as a rigid, one-directional sequence rather than a genuine, backward-looping process.

title: "Eating the Frog"
snippet: The practice of tackling the highest-value, hardest task first, rather than deferring it.

title: "How Might We" (HMW)
snippet: A reframing technique transforming a problem statement into an open-ended, optimistic question to widen the candidate solution space.

title: "Loudest Voice Wins"
snippet: The failure pattern of prioritizing a pain point based on how forcefully it was raised, rather than its actual severity/frequency.

title: "Most Recent Complaint Wins"
snippet: The failure pattern of prioritizing whichever pain point was most recently raised, rather than a systematic comparison.

title: "Org Chart as Navigation" (Failure Pattern)
snippet: Structuring a product's navigation around internal team/department boundaries rather than validated user mental models.

title: "PM as Design Dictator" (Failure Pattern)
snippet: Using UX knowledge to unilaterally prescribe specific design solutions rather than raising concerns and deferring execution to design expertise.

title: "PRD as One-Way Document" (Failure Pattern)
snippet: Treating a PRD as a final, unquestionable decree rather than a living, collaboratively refined artifact.

title: "Prioritization Theater" (Failure Pattern)
snippet: Applying a formal-looking prioritization framework to justify a decision already made for other reasons.

title: "Story as a Disguised Task" (Failure Pattern)
snippet: Writing technical work in user-story grammar without genuine standalone value to a named persona.

title: What is the "who creates the value" test?
snippet: Ask who built the thing that made a user's experience good — your own team (feature product) or a third party using your tools (platform).

title: Name the four layers of the Leverage Stack in order.
snippet: Core Product → Developer Surface → Marketplace → Ecosystem.

title: Why can a healthy end-user engagement metric mask a decaying platform?
snippet: Existing integrations keep working even as new developer investment quietly stalls, so end-user dashboards lag the real signal.

title: What is a cross-side network effect?
snippet: A loop where growth in one population (builders or end users) increases the platform's value for the other population, and vice versa.

title: What does the Platform Readiness Checklist assess?
snippet: Whether a Developer Surface (Layer 2) is stable and trustworthy enough to support Marketplace or Ecosystem investment (Layers 3–4).

title: Why did the SaaS company's Marketplace fail in the Case Study?
snippet: It invested in a public Layer 3 marketplace while its Layer 2 API was still unversioned and prone to undocumented breaking changes.

title: Name two things that are typically in tension between developers and end users.
snippet: Developers want stability and advance notice; end users often want frequent, visible change and rapid iteration.

title: Why should an API be understood as a promise rather than an interface?
snippet: Because developers build production systems assuming today's behavior will hold, without visibility into your roadmap — a broken assumption has real downstream cost.

title: Name the three Promise Tiers in order of stability.
snippet: Stable Core, Versioned Standard, Experimental/Beta.

title: What does semantic versioning communicate that a plain version number doesn't?
snippet: The size and safety of a change — patch (bug fix), minor (additive), major (breaking) — so developers know how much risk a change carries.

title: Why did labeling the webhook field as "internal implementation detail" fail in the Case Study?
snippet: Dozens of partners had, in practice, already come to depend on it for reconciliation, so it functioned as a Tier 1 promise even though it was never classified as one.

title: What is idempotency and why does it matter for API design?
snippet: The property that repeating an operation produces the same result without unintended side effects — critical so retry logic after network failures doesn't create duplicates.

title: What should block a launch, according to the API Design Checklist?
snippet: An endpoint with no explicit Promise Tier classification — an unclassified endpoint is a promise made by default without anyone deciding what it is.

title: What converts an abstract stability claim into an operational guarantee?
snippet: Semantic versioning combined with a published, enforced deprecation policy.

title: What makes a marketplace "two-sided" rather than just having two user types?
snippet: Each population derives no value from the platform without sufficient presence of the other — the two sides are mutually dependent for the core value proposition.

title: What is the chicken-and-egg problem?
snippet: Neither side of a marketplace wants to join until the other side is already present in sufficient numbers.

title: Name three strategies for solving the chicken-and-egg problem.
snippet: Single-player mode, geographic/niche concentration, subsidizing the harder-to-acquire side, or seeding with owned supply/demand.

title: Why is liquidity a better marketplace health metric than registered-user count?
snippet: A marketplace can have huge registered-user counts on both sides with almost no successful matches — liquidity measures whether the core value proposition is actually being delivered.

title: In the Case Study, why did tripling demand-side signups hurt the marketplace?
snippet: Supply hadn't grown proportionally, so the constrained side (supply) was flooded with more demand than it could serve, worsening fill rate and client satisfaction.

title: What three questions does the Two-Sided Balance Model ask before approving a growth initiative?
snippet: Which side's leading indicators are weak? Is the initiative targeted at the constrained side? Could it worsen the imbalance by growing the abundant side further?

title: Why should supply-side and demand-side signals never be blended into one aggregate health score?
snippet: Blending obscures which specific side actually needs attention, leading to misdirected growth investment.

title: What is the actual constraint on data-informed decision-making at scale, according to this lesson?
snippet: Organizational metric trust, not the volume of available data.

title: Name the five stages of the Metric Provenance Chain in order.
snippet: Instrumentation, Validation, Definition Consensus, Trusted Metric, Decision.

title: What is metric definition drift?
snippet: The gradual, often silent divergence between a metric's original intended meaning and what it currently actually measures.

title: What does dashboard fragmentation indicate about an organization?
snippet: That its Metric Provenance Chain is broken somewhere between Definition Consensus and Trusted Metric status.

title: In the Case Study, why didn't either retention dashboard get flagged as "wrong"?
snippet: Both were internally valid and consistently computed — the failure was the absence of company-wide Definition Consensus and a designated single source of truth, not a calculation error in either dashboard.

title: Why is an executive's personal dashboard not automatically a Trusted Metric?
snippet: Organizational seniority is not a substitute for provenance — any metric must pass through Validation and Definition Consensus regardless of its source.

title: What should a PM do if a metric fails the Single Source of Truth check?
snippet: Treat it as an active organizational risk — decisions may currently be resting on incompatible versions of the same nominal number.

title: Why can a technically excellent model still be wrong for a product?
snippet: Its optimization target is a proxy for the real business outcome, and proxies can diverge from that outcome in ways invisible during model development.

title: Name the four zones of the Ownership Zones Model.
snippet: Problem Framing (PM), Model Development (Data Science), Output Interpretation (Shared), Product Decision and Deployment (PM).

title: Why is the precision/recall trade-off a product decision, not a purely technical one?
snippet: It depends on the relative business cost of false positives versus false negatives, information only the PM typically has.

title: What is the base-rate problem, as illustrated by the churn example?
snippet: When the positive class (e.g., churners) is rare, a model that simply predicts "no one churns" can still score high on accuracy, making accuracy alone misleading.

title: What went wrong in the Overzealous Churn Model case study?
snippet: The model was framed as recall-oriented without quantifying customer success's real outreach capacity, producing more false positives than the team could handle.

title: What must a PM supply before model development begins, per the Collaboration Checklist?
snippet: The business decision the model informs, relative error costs, capacity constraints of downstream teams, and a minimum acceptable performance threshold.

title: Why shouldn't a model's probabilistic output be treated as a fact?
snippet: A "churn probability of 0.7" is an estimate requiring interpretation (Zone 3), not equivalent to certainty that the customer will churn.

title: Why can a recommender optimized purely for short-term engagement produce a filter bubble?
snippet: It learns that showing more of what already worked reliably produces the next positive response, narrowing exposure over time even as short-term metrics improve.

title: Name the three zones of the Discovery Frontier model.
snippet: Known Preference Zone, Discovery Frontier, Irrelevant Zone.

title: Why must diversity and novelty metrics be tracked alongside accuracy metrics?
snippet: Accuracy-style metrics (precision, CTR) cannot detect a narrowing filter bubble, since they only measure whether known-preference predictions were correct.

title: What is the cold-start problem?
snippet: The difficulty of generating relevant recommendations for new users or new catalog items due to insufficient interaction history.

title: Why did skip rate improve while 90-day retention declined in the Case Study?
snippet: The recommender optimized for immediate skip avoidance by serving increasingly narrow, safe, already-liked content, which reduced skips short-term but bored users over a longer horizon.

title: Name two mitigation strategies for the cold-start problem.
snippet: Onboarding preference surveys for explicit signal, and popularity-based or content-based fallback recommendations until behavioral data accumulates.

title: Why is filter bubble damage often invisible on short-term dashboards?
snippet: It operates on a longer retention timescale than daily engagement metrics track, requiring long-horizon monitoring like the Smile Curve to detect.

title: Why is "detect and remove" an insufficient governance strategy?
snippet: No detection system is perfectly accurate, so treating removal as the only response converts every false positive into a full, often irreversible harm to an honest participant.

title: Name the four steps of the Escalation Staircase in order.
snippet: Soft Signal, Restriction, Suspension, Termination.

title: Why should lower escalation steps be reversible?
snippet: To limit the damage a false positive can cause to an honest participant, since detection confidence at lower steps is, by design, lower.

title: Why is an appeals process a structural requirement, not a courtesy?
snippet: Because any system that acknowledges its own imperfect accuracy must provide a path to correct the false positives it will inevitably produce.

title: What went wrong in the Automated Seller Purge case study?
snippet: A moderate-confidence detection signal was connected directly to permanent termination with no graduated steps, paired with a non-functional appeals process, harming honest sellers and damaging marketplace liquidity.

title: How does trust and safety enforcement relate to the precision/recall trade-off from Lesson 65?
snippet: It is a high-stakes application of the same trade-off — maximizing catch rate (recall) mechanically increases false positives against honest participants, a cost that must be deliberately weighed.

title: Why should enforcement outcomes be monitored over a long time horizon?
snippet: Patterns of disproportionate or biased enforcement against specific participant segments can take considerable time to surface, similar to filter bubble damage in Lesson 66.

title: Why does platform-scale technical debt differ in kind from team-level technical debt?
snippet: Dependents are frequently external, numerous, and hard to fully enumerate, turning an internal trade-off into an ecosystem-wide trust obligation.

title: Name the four phases of the Sunset Runway in order.
snippet: Dependency Inventory, Announcement & Dual-Run, Active Migration Support, Decommission.

title: Why do registered-integration inventories often undercount true dependency?
snippet: They miss undocumented workarounds, third-party intermediaries, and shared-key usage patterns that don't show up as distinct, directly registered integrations.

title: What is the purpose of a dual-run period?
snippet: To decouple the platform's readiness to retire something from each dependent's individual readiness to migrate, avoiding a forced synchronized cutover.

title: What went wrong in the Underestimated Cutover case study?
snippet: The dependency inventory relied only on registered API keys, missing hundreds of downstream customers behind a third-party vendor's shared integration, and decommission proceeded on calendar date regardless of their migration status.

title: Why should Phase 4 (Decommission) be gated on migration progress rather than calendar date alone?
snippet: A fixed date regardless of actual completion converts a planned transition into a forced, disruptive cutover for anyone who hasn't finished migrating.

title: Why is Phase 3 (Active Migration Support) necessary beyond simply announcing a deprecation?
snippet: Passive announcement alone tends to leave a long tail of dependents unaware or unprepared until the deadline arrives.

title: Why do internal platforms require the same product discipline as external-facing platforms?
snippet: Their Layer 2 Developer Surface, per the Leverage Stack, serves internal engineers just as an external platform's serves outside developers — the same promise and friction dynamics apply.

title: Why does the "we're all colleagues" assumption fail for internal platforms?
snippet: Internal engineers do have an alternative to tolerating friction — quietly building their own workaround — which imposes real, often invisible costs on the company.

title: What is a shadow platform?
snippet: Parallel, duplicated infrastructure built by internal teams frustrated with an official internal platform's friction, usually without formally complaining first.

title: Why is the absence of complaints not reliable evidence of a healthy internal platform?
snippet: Silence can indicate that frustrated teams have quietly disengaged and built around the problem instead of raising it.

title: What went wrong in the Duplicated Deployment Pipeline case study?
snippet: Two teams independently built workaround deployment scripts due to onboarding friction, with no formal complaint, and the duplication went undetected for nearly a year until a security audit found it.

title: Name two concrete metrics for measuring internal developer experience.
snippet: Time-to-first-success and support ticket volume/resolution time (plus periodic satisfaction surveys).

title: What should an internal platform team actively monitor for, beyond just tracking friction points?
snippet: The emergence of shadow platforms elsewhere in the organization, since their appearance is direct evidence of unaddressed friction.

title: Name all nine Module 7 mental models in the order they were introduced.
snippet: Leverage Stack, Promise Tiers, Two-Sided Balance Model, Metric Provenance Chain, Ownership Zones Model, Discovery Frontier, Escalation Staircase, Sunset Runway, Friction Ledger.

title: What is the Platform Health Radar?
snippet: An integrated diagnostic tool that assesses a platform across all nine Module 7 dimensions simultaneously, rather than applying one model in isolation.

title: How does Promise Tiers relate to the Leverage Stack?
snippet: Promise Tiers specifically governs Layer 2 (Developer Surface) of the Leverage Stack, formalizing what stability commitments mean at that layer.

title: How does the Discovery Frontier relate to the Ownership Zones Model?
snippet: The Discovery Frontier is a specialized, high-stakes application of the Ownership Zones Model's error-cost logic to ranking and personalization decisions specifically.

title: Why did the Multi-Front Ecosystem Decline case study require more than one model to diagnose correctly?
snippet: The true cause was a compounding failure across Promise Tiers (a broken API commitment), Escalation Staircase (a governance enforcement failure), and Metric Provenance Chain (a partially obscuring metric drift) simultaneously.

title: What is the risk of applying only the first model that seems to fit a platform symptom?
snippet: Most real platform incidents involve failures across more than one axis, and stopping the diagnosis early misses compounding causes.

title: What does genuine "platform judgment" mean, per this synthesis lesson?
snippet: The applied skill of recognizing which combination of models fits a real, ambiguous situation — not simply memorizing each model individually.

title: Why can't a vision statement alone guide near-term execution decisions?
snippet: Its necessary abstraction and stability mean it doesn't specify what would count as evidence the organization is succeeding or failing.

title: Name the four levels of the Strategy Cascade in order.
snippet: Vision, Strategic Bets, Roadmap Initiatives, Success Metrics.

title: What three properties make a Strategic Bet genuinely falsifiable?
snippet: A specific hypothesis, committed real resources, and pre-defined success criteria specified in advance.

title: What are the three Horizons in the Three Horizons framework?
snippet: Horizon 1 (Core), Horizon 2 (Adjacent), Horizon 3 (Transformational).

title: Why did the collaboration pivot in the Case Study become unfalsifiable?
snippet: The organization skipped the Strategic Bet layer, jumping directly from vision to initiatives, so no pre-defined evidence existed to judge success or failure.

title: What risk does an all-Horizon-1 portfolio carry?
snippet: Long-term stagnation, since no adjacent or transformational bets exist to sustain growth beyond the current core business.

title: What risk does judging Horizon 3 bets by the same near-term metrics as Horizon 1 carry?
snippet: Premature cancellation of transformational bets before they have a fair chance to prove themselves.

title: Why is enterprise readiness a distinct category from "more features"?
snippet: It establishes organizational trust and control — security, administrative oversight, reliability, integration — rather than serving an individual user's core task directly.

title: Name the four rungs of the Enterprise Adoption Ladder.
snippet: Pilot, Departmental Adoption, Organization-Wide Rollout, Mission-Critical Entrenchment.

title: Name the four categories of enterprise readiness capability.
snippet: Security and compliance, administrative control, reliability and support commitments, integration capability.

title: Why couldn't strong user satisfaction metrics unblock the security review stall in the Case Study?
snippet: Security review criteria (certifications, access control, audit logs) are entirely separate from user satisfaction, and central IT/security stakeholders were never part of the original grassroots adoption.

title: Why can a single missing enterprise readiness category block a deal regardless of strength elsewhere?
snippet: Procurement and security review processes typically treat each category as a separate, non-negotiable gate rather than allowing compensation across categories.

title: Why should enterprise readiness capabilities often be built proactively rather than reactively?
snippet: Certifications and related capabilities often require significant lead time to obtain, and waiting until a specific deal demands them can cause avoidable delays.

title: What distinguishes isolated enthusiasm from genuine organizational rollout progress?
snippet: Isolated enthusiasm reflects Rung 1/2 success among individual users, while organizational rollout requires engagement and approval from Rung 3 gatekeepers like central IT and security, who evaluate entirely different criteria.

title: Why do B2B purchasing decisions typically involve multiple stakeholder roles, unlike consumer purchases?
snippet: In B2B, the functions of using, deciding, and paying for a product are frequently distributed across different people with different incentives, unlike a consumer purchase where one person fulfills all roles.

title: Name the four roles of the Stakeholder Compass.
snippet: Champion, Economic Buyer, Technical Evaluator, End User.

title: What is the Champion-Without-Authority Trap?
snippet: Over-relying on a genuinely enthusiastic Champion's account of deal progress without directly engaging the Economic Buyer or Technical Evaluator, who hold actual approval authority.

title: What does the Economic Buyer primarily evaluate a purchase on?
snippet: Return on investment and total cost relative to alternatives, often with limited firsthand exposure to the product itself.

title: Why did the Champion Who Couldn't Deliver case study's deal ultimately stall?
snippet: The startup invested exclusively in the enthusiastic Champion, never directly engaging the Economic Buyer (who controlled budget) or the Technical Evaluator (who required security review), both of whom held actual approval authority.

title: Why should the Technical Evaluator be engaged early rather than late in a B2B sales process?
snippet: Given their veto-level authority, late engagement risks a costly, momentum-killing stall at exactly the point a deal seemed closest to completion.

title: Why might a single person occupy multiple Stakeholder Compass roles simultaneously?
snippet: In smaller organizations, one person (e.g., a small business owner) may be Economic Buyer, Technical Evaluator, and End User all at once.

title: Why does land-and-expand require deliberate packaging design, not just a sales strategy?
snippet: The initial land must be low-friction and deliver genuine standalone value, while the packaging must also create natural expansion triggers — both require intentional structure, not just sales execution.

title: Name the three parts of the Expansion Wedge.
snippet: Land Tier, Expansion Triggers, Enterprise Tier.

title: Name the three types of expansion triggers.
snippet: Seat-based, usage-based, and feature-gated.

title: What risk does an overly generous Land Tier create?
snippet: It eliminates the natural pressure to expand, producing strong adoption metrics that mask a failing business model, as in the Land That Never Expanded case study.

title: What risk does an overly restrictive Land Tier create?
snippet: It prevents the initial land motion from succeeding at all, since Rung 1 of the Enterprise Adoption Ladder requires genuine standalone value.

title: Why should Enterprise Tier capability match Rung 3/4 needs specifically, rather than an arbitrary "premium" bundle?
snippet: Because the Enterprise Tier must satisfy the Technical Evaluator and Economic Buyer roles from Lesson 73, whose actual needs are security, admin control, reliability, and integration.

title: What went wrong in the Land That Never Expanded case study?
snippet: The free tier had unlimited seats and nearly the full feature set, eliminating every natural expansion trigger, and no genuine enterprise tier or enterprise-readiness capability had ever been built.

title: Why is a current market advantage not automatically a competitive moat?
snippet: A moat requires structural difficulty of replication, even for well-resourced competitors, not merely an unchallenged lead that hasn't yet been seriously tested.

title: What are the two dimensions of the Moat Durability Matrix?
snippet: Replication difficulty and natural erosion risk.

title: Name the five common moat categories.
snippet: Network effects, switching costs, economies of scale, brand and trust, proprietary assets.

title: Why are network effects more fragile than commonly assumed?
snippet: Multi-homing allows participants to use a competing platform with minimal cost, undermining the "must join the biggest network" logic network effects rely on.

title: What went wrong in the Multi-Homed Marketplace case study?
snippet: The incumbent assumed its network effect was a permanent, high-difficulty moat, but low-cost multi-homing allowed a competitor to capture valuable participants without fully displacing the incumbent.

title: Why should switching costs be evaluated from the customer's perspective rather than the vendor's?
snippet: A switching cost that feels significant to the vendor may feel much smaller to a genuinely dissatisfied customer, especially if a competitor offers migration assistance.

title: Why is brand recognition distinct from brand trust as a moat?
snippet: Awareness of a brand does not guarantee the deep customer confidence needed to resist a comparable competitor's offer; only genuine trust functions as a real moat.

title: Why is poor integration, rather than flawed strategy, the more common cause of M&A value destruction?
snippet: An acquisition's value is realized or destroyed over the months and years of integration following the deal, not at the moment the deal closes.

title: Name the four points on the Integration Continuum.
snippet: Preserve, Selective Integration, Full Absorption, Sunset and Migrate.

title: Name the four common strategic rationales for an acquisition.
snippet: Talent acquisition, technology acquisition, customer base acquisition, market consolidation.

title: Why is premature Full Absorption such a common mistake?
snippet: Internal stakeholders often prefer a unified codebase and structure for its own sake, regardless of whether the acquisition's actual rationale calls for full integration.

title: What went wrong in the Rushed Absorption case study?
snippet: The acquisition's rationale was customer-base retention, but leadership forced rapid Full Absorption without understanding what drove customer loyalty, causing significant churn.

title: Why should acquired customer migration follow Sunset Runway discipline from Lesson 68?
snippet: Acquired customers are genuine dependents whose loyalty drivers and workflow needs must be understood before a migration timeline is set, just like external API dependents.

title: Why does ambiguous communication with an acquired team accelerate departures?
snippet: Uncertainty about which integration approach applies to them creates anxiety that can drive talent away regardless of which approach ultimately proves correct.

title: Why does applying uniform revenue metrics across a portfolio produce a category error?
snippet: An early-stage Horizon 3 bet is structurally too early to demonstrate the scale evidence a mature Horizon 1 business reasonably should, making revenue comparison inappropriate at that stage.

title: Name the four validation stages on the Portfolio Health Grid.
snippet: Concept, Prototype, Pilot, Scale.

title: What is the difference between validated learning and a vanity metric?
snippet: Validated learning tests a specific, falsifiable hypothesis and confirms or disconfirms it; a vanity metric merely looks encouraging without testing anything meaningful.

title: What are the two failure modes caused by metric mismatch?
snippet: Premature cancellation of promising early bets, and prolonged survival of genuinely failing bets.

title: Why was the Pilot-stage subscription initiative killed in the Prematurely Killed Experiment case study?
snippet: It was evaluated using a Horizon 1-appropriate absolute revenue contribution metric, a Scale-stage standard the Pilot-stage bet could not reasonably meet yet, despite genuinely earning validated learning at its actual stage.

title: What appropriate evidence should a Concept-stage bet be evaluated against?
snippet: A clearly articulated, falsifiable hypothesis and a designed initial test — not revenue or user growth targets.

title: Why should progression between validation stages be earned by evidence rather than assumed by elapsed time?
snippet: A bet should advance to the next stage only because specific validated learning milestones have actually been met, not simply because time has passed.

title: What is "not invented here" syndrome?
snippet: An organizational tendency to prefer building a capability internally over acquiring it externally, often for reasons unrelated to genuine strategic advantage.

title: What are the two axes of the Capability Sourcing Matrix?
snippet: Genuine competitive differentiation and external market maturity.

title: When should a capability generally be built internally?
snippet: When it is genuinely central to the company's moat and no mature external solution already exists.

title: Why does evaluating a build decision on initial cost alone understate its true cost?
snippet: It ignores ongoing Friction Ledger maintenance burden and eventual Sunset Runway retirement cost over the capability's full lifecycle.

title: What went wrong in the Custom Analytics Platform case study?
snippet: A build decision that was reasonable when the external market was immature was never revisited as the market matured, allowing a non-differentiating internal platform to consume growing resources long after superior external alternatives existed.

title: Why should existing internal builds be periodically reassessed?
snippet: A build decision that was genuinely correct when made can become outdated as external markets mature, and organizational discomfort with reversing prior investment shouldn't prevent honest reassessment.

title: What quadrant of the Capability Sourcing Matrix calls for a Partner approach?
snippet: High differentiation combined with a mature external market, where integrating an external provider while retaining differentiation elsewhere is often preferable to building from scratch.

title: Why is a direct price discount often a poor negotiation trade?
snippet: It establishes a new baseline expectation for future renewals and can become a credible anchor other customers use in their own negotiations, compounding its cost over time.

title: What are the two dimensions of the Concession Exchange Map?
snippet: Vendor cost and customer value.

title: Name two examples of low-vendor-cost, high-customer-value concessions.
snippet: Extended payment terms (e.g., net-60 or net-90) and flexible contract start dates aligned to the customer's fiscal year.

title: Why might a customer's stated concern about "cost" actually be about something else?
snippet: The underlying issue might be cash flow timing, contract risk, or implementation confidence rather than headline price itself, addressable through a non-price lever.

title: What went wrong in the Discount That Became the Floor case study?
snippet: A large, precedent-setting price discount was granted to close a strategically significant deal without exploring non-price alternatives, and it became an expected baseline for renewals and other customers' negotiations.

title: Why should concessions be matched to the specific stakeholder motivating the request?
snippet: A concession satisfying the Economic Buyer's concern may not address a Technical Evaluator's separate concern, per the Stakeholder Compass from Lesson 73, leaving the actual objection unresolved.

title: Why should precedent risk be explicitly documented before granting a significant concession?
snippet: Because the compounding cost of a concession is easy to overlook in the moment, given the immediate pressure to close the specific deal in front of the negotiator.

title: Name all nine Module 8 mental models in the order they were introduced.
snippet: Strategy Cascade, Enterprise Adoption Ladder, Stakeholder Compass, Expansion Wedge, Moat Durability Matrix, Integration Continuum, Portfolio Health Grid, Capability Sourcing Matrix, Concession Exchange Map.

title: What is the Strategic Judgment Radar?
snippet: An integrated diagnostic tool assessing a strategic situation across all nine Module 8 dimensions simultaneously, rather than applying one model in isolation.

title: How does the Enterprise Adoption Ladder relate to the Stakeholder Compass?
snippet: They describe the same B2B adoption process from complementary angles — rungs of organizational progress, and the specific people who gate that progress at each rung.

title: How does the Moat Durability Matrix relate to the Capability Sourcing Matrix?
snippet: Genuine competitive differentiation, assessed by the Moat Durability Matrix, is one of the two core axes the Capability Sourcing Matrix uses to recommend Build, Buy, or Partner.

title: Why did the Multi-Front Strategic Stall case study require more than one model to diagnose correctly?
snippet: The true cause was a shared pattern across an unmatched acquisition integration, incomplete stakeholder engagement in stalled accounts, and premature evaluation of a maturing bet — three seemingly unrelated symptoms with one underlying root cause.

title: What is the risk of applying only the first model that seems to fit a strategic symptom?
snippet: Most significant strategic problems involve failures across more than one axis, and stopping the diagnosis early misses compounding causes.

title: What does genuine "advanced strategic judgment" mean, per this synthesis lesson?
snippet: The applied skill of recognizing which combination of models fits a real, ambiguous situation — not simply memorizing each model individually.

title: Why must regulatory compliance often shape product architecture from the outset in regulated industries?
snippet: Structural requirements like audit trails and mandatory human review steps are far more costly to retrofit than to design in from the beginning.

title: Name the four layers of the Regulatory Surface Map.
snippet: Data, Process, Outcome, Liability.

title: Why can a well-documented process still fail regulatory compliance?
snippet: Process Layer compliance doesn't guarantee Outcome Layer compliance — a carefully documented decision process can still produce an impermissible result, such as a discriminatory outcome.

title: How do human-in-the-loop requirements connect to the Ownership Zones Model from Lesson 65?
snippet: They formalize Zone 4's discipline — that a model's output shouldn't be treated as an automatic action — into a legal obligation rather than an optional best practice.

title: What two regulatory gaps did the Undocumented Lending Decision case study reveal?
snippet: A discriminatory disparity in approval rates across demographic groups (Outcome Layer), and a missing mandatory human review step for denied applications (Liability Layer) — despite thorough Process Layer documentation.

title: Why does the Liability Layer often shape a product's core architecture directly?
snippet: A system that cannot reconstruct its own decision history after the fact cannot support the accountability assignment regulation frequently requires.

title: Why is ongoing regulatory monitoring necessary even after a product is compliant at launch?
snippet: Regulations in healthcare, finance, and government contexts change over time, and a product can drift out of compliance as rules evolve.

title: What is data minimization?
snippet: The principle that an organization should collect only data genuinely necessary for a specific, disclosed purpose, and retain it only as long as that purpose requires.

title: Name the four stages of the Data Flow Risk Map.
snippet: Collection, Storage, Processing, Sharing.

title: Why is a contractual data processing agreement insufficient protection on its own?
snippet: A contract establishes legal recourse after a third party's security failure but does not technically prevent that failure from occurring in the first place.

title: What is "purpose creep"?
snippet: Using data collected for one stated purpose for an unrelated purpose later, without updated disclosure or renewed consent — a minimization violation even on legitimately collected data.

title: What went wrong in the Third-Party Data Exposure case study?
snippet: The company shared far more health data than its analytics purpose required, relying solely on a contractual agreement with no technical safeguards, leaving it exposed when the third party's own security failed.

title: Why should right-to-deletion capability be designed in from the outset?
snippet: A system not originally built to track where an individual's data has propagated is far harder to retrofit with the ability to locate and delete that data later.

title: Why is encryption alone insufficient security without access control?
snippet: Encrypted data broadly accessible for internal convenience still carries meaningful risk from internal misuse or a compromised internal account bypassing encryption's protection.

title: Why does hardware development carry a fundamentally different risk profile than software?
snippet: Software assumes mistakes can typically be corrected through a subsequent deployment, but hardware has genuine, irreversible commitment points, like tooling and mass production, after which a flaw can no longer be simply patched.

title: Name the five stages of the Commitment Curve.
snippet: Concept, Prototype, Tooling Commitment, Mass Production, Shipped to Customers.

title: What can OTA (over-the-air) updates correct, and what can't they correct?
snippet: They can correct firmware and software issues, but they cannot correct genuinely physical hardware flaws, like a defective battery or sensor.

title: Why should validation rigor scale with proximity to a Commitment Curve stage?
snippet: The cost of reversing a decision increases sharply near commitment points like tooling, so more scrutiny is needed immediately before these thresholds than earlier in development.

title: What went wrong in the Unfixable Battery Flaw case study?
snippet: A physical battery design issue identified during prototype testing was assumed to be firmware-correctable and given insufficient validation before tooling commitment, but it was actually a genuine physical flaw requiring a costly recall.

title: Why should firmware update capability be designed into a product from the outset?
snippet: Retrofitting OTA update capability into a device not originally designed to support it is considerably more difficult than building it in from the start.

title: What is the "Physical vs. Firmware Classification" step, and why does it matter?
snippet: It's the practice of determining whether an identified flaw is a genuinely physical issue or a software-correctable one — getting this wrong, as in the Case Study, can lead to a costly assumption that a problem can be fixed after shipment when it genuinely cannot.

title: Why can't model quality be reduced to a single number?
snippet: Capability and reliability are distinct and can diverge sharply, requiring different product responses.

title: What does the high-capability/low-reliability quadrant call for?
snippet: Human-in-the-loop assist mode, not full automation.

title: Why must evals run continuously?
snippet: Model and prompt changes shift behavior, so pre-launch evaluation alone doesn't guarantee ongoing quality.

title: What went wrong in the Automated Refund Assistant case study?
snippet: A quadrant-B task (high capability, imperfect reliability) was shipped at full automation with no human review, leading to hallucination-driven refund errors.

title: Why do traditional QA assumptions break down for generative AI products?
snippet: Traditional QA assumes deterministic behavior — same input, same output, forever, unless the code changes. Generative models can produce different outputs for the same input, and behavior can shift with silent provider-side updates, so a passing test suite doesn't guarantee ongoing quality the way it does for deterministic software.

title: What is "quadrant drift" and why does it matter?
snippet: A feature's real capability/reliability position shifting over time — even without any deliberate product change — as usage patterns diversify or the underlying model updates. It matters because a feature correctly classified as quadrant A at launch can silently become quadrant B, which is why the AI Product Readiness Checklist should be re-run periodically, not filled out once.

title: Why can aggregate accuracy mask disparity?
snippet: A model can perform very differently across subgroups while its overall accuracy number looks acceptable.

title: What are the four steps of the Fairness Audit Loop?
snippet: Define equity metric, measure across groups, diagnose disparity source, remediate — then repeat.

title: Why is adjusting output thresholds by group a superficial fix?
snippet: It doesn't address the root cause, such as biased training data, and can mask or complicate the underlying problem.

title: What went wrong in the Biased Hiring Screener case study?
snippet: Aggregate accuracy masked disparity traceable to historically biased training data, never diagnosed at its root, with no ongoing measurement or appeal process.

title: Why can't a team simply instruct engineers to "make the model fair"?
snippet: There is no single, universally agreed mathematical definition of fairness — demographic parity and equalized error rates can be mutually incompatible for the same decision, so the team must explicitly choose and document which definition is appropriate given the real-world consequences.

title: In the Biased Hiring Screener case, why was excluding gender and disability status from model inputs not sufficient?
snippet: University attended and employment gaps functioned as proxy variables correlated with the excluded characteristics, allowing the model to reconstruct much of the same discriminatory pattern indirectly.

title: Why is translation insufficient for genuine international scaling?
snippet: Deeper adaptation layers — cultural fit, payment methods, regulatory requirements — are invisible from a translation-only perspective and can block adoption regardless of translation quality.

title: Name the four levels of the Adaptation Depth Model.
snippet: Surface, Cultural, Structural, Product.

title: Why is payment method localization commonly underestimated?
snippet: Payment infrastructure varies sharply by country, and a product supporting only home-market payment methods can see adoption blocked entirely in a new market.

title: What went wrong in the Payment Wall case study?
snippet: Excellent Surface and Cultural adaptation still failed to drive conversion because the product only supported credit card payments in a market where mobile-money and cash-on-delivery dominated.

title: Why is Cultural adaptation harder to verify than Surface translation?
snippet: Translation has an objective correctness standard, but cultural fit (color meaning, imagery, communication style) has no equivalent checkpoint — a product can be linguistically flawless and culturally tone-deaf at the same time.

title: Why did the Payment Wall team take a long time to diagnose their conversion problem?
snippet: Their funnel analytics weren't broken down by payment method, so the drop-off concentrated at the payment step was masked within an otherwise strong-looking aggregate funnel.

title: Why must communication and containment proceed in parallel during a crisis?
snippet: Silence during a visible failure compounds user anxiety and trust erosion, so acknowledgment shouldn't wait for full technical resolution.

title: What are the four phases of the Crisis Response Timeline?
snippet: Detect and Triage, Contain and Communicate (in parallel), Resolve, Postmortem and Prevent.

title: Why is providing an overconfident resolution timeline risky during a crisis?
snippet: If missed, it creates a second, avoidable broken promise on top of the original incident, echoing the Promise Tiers discipline from Lesson 62.

title: What went wrong in the Silent Outage case study?
snippet: Communication was delayed for hours while engineering investigated, and the eventual update gave an overconfident timeline that was subsequently missed.

title: Why does severity classification need to happen before communication and technical fixing begin in earnest?
snippet: Without it, a team can under-communicate a genuinely serious incident or over-communicate a minor one, and severity also determines who needs to be involved (legal, security, executives) from the outset.

title: What is a "narrative vacuum" and why does it matter in crisis communication?
snippet: The gap left by silence during a visible incident — affected users and observers will fill it with their own assumptions, usually worse than reality, before an official explanation arrives.

title: Why does reactive headcount addition fail to solve overextended PM scope?
snippet: It tends to preserve an existing PM's scope while adding new PMs only for new initiatives, leaving established areas overextended.

title: What does the Coherence Span Model track?
snippet: A PM's ownership span by initiative count and interdependency complexity.

title: Why is adding support insufficient for an overextended PM?
snippet: Support roles don't solve the underlying coherence problem, since the original PM remains the single point of prioritization and decision-making judgment.

title: What went wrong in the Overextended Owner case study?
snippet: A founding PM's scope grew to a dozen loosely related initiatives through reactive addition, causing delayed decisions and unsupported team decisions, never addressed until the situation became acute.

title: Why is this overextension failure pattern so persistent across growing companies, even though it's recognizable in hindsight?
snippet: Splitting ownership can feel like a demotion to both the PM and leadership, and overextension accumulates gradually with no single obvious trigger for a structural review — unlike hiring, which has a clear trigger.

title: How did the founding PM in the Overextended Owner case study react to having their scope split?
snippet: They reported relief rather than diminishment, a detail the company later used to reframe splitting conversations as scope-appropriate role design rather than a judgment on past performance.

title: Why doesn't AI capability at drafting eliminate the need for PM judgment?
snippet: A tool can produce a fluent, polished draft while missing exactly the accountability and context-dependent judgment call that made the task worth doing.

title: What are the four quadrants of the PM Judgment Reserve model?
snippet: Execution/high-automatability, execution/low-automatability, judgment/AI-augmentable, judgment/irreducibly human.

title: Why is polish not the same as correctness?
snippet: A fluent, well-organized AI output can still contain a judgment error invisible to a reviewer who stops actively exercising judgment because it already looks finished.

title: What went wrong in the Unreviewed Roadmap case study?
snippet: An AI-generated roadmap weighted feedback by raw frequency, missing a low-volume but high-stakes enterprise concern the PM would ordinarily have caught through direct judgment.

title: Why is judgment-reserve erosion gradual and hard to notice from the inside?
snippet: It happens through a series of individually reasonable, small time-saving deferrals rather than one obvious moment of abdication — the same gradual-accumulation dynamic as Lesson 88's coherence overextension.

title: What is the "felt-redundancy trap" described in the Unreviewed Roadmap case study?
snippet: The mistaken sense that re-deriving a judgment independently is unnecessary because a tool's output already looks thorough — misleading because the tool never had visibility into the specific strategic context that judgment required.

title: What does this final lesson add to the curriculum's roster of mental models?
snippet: No new diagnostic model — it integrates everything already built into the Integrated Practice Wheel.

title: What are the three outer rings of the Integrated Practice Wheel?
snippet: The Platform Health Radar (mechanism), the Strategic Judgment Radar (direction), and Module 9's specialized domain lenses (context).

title: What sits at the center of the Integrated Practice Wheel?
snippet: The personal product philosophy first articulated in Lesson 60.

title: What did the Full-Spectrum Incident case study require diagnostically?
snippet: Crisis communication (Lesson 87), AI reliability and fairness diagnosis (Lessons 84–85), regulatory compliance (Lesson 81), and international adaptation review (Lesson 86) — simultaneously.
